body:
The Chauri Chaura incident

On 4 February 1922, a confrontation occurred at Chauri Chaura, in the Gorakhpur district of the United Provinces, now in Uttar Pradesh. A demonstration developed into a violent clash with the police. The crowd set fire to a police station, and 22 policemen were killed.

The incident was important because Gandhi had made non-violence an essential condition of the Non-Cooperation Movement. He believed that a mass movement relying on satyagraha could not achieve its purpose through attacks and retaliation.

Why was the movement withdrawn?

Gandhi concluded that the movement was becoming violent in several places and that many participants required more preparation in non-violent discipline. Continuing the agitation without that discipline risked turning it into a struggle conducted by methods he opposed.

The Congress Working Committee met at Bardoli in Gujarat on 11–12 February 1922. It resolved to suspend the proposed mass civil disobedience campaign. The wider Non-Cooperation Movement was consequently brought to an end in February 1922.

The decision was controversial. Some nationalists believed the movement still possessed considerable public support and that withdrawal would weaken political momentum. Gandhi nevertheless maintained that the means of the struggle were inseparable from its objective.

The date and place distinction

Chauri Chaura, Uttar Pradesh: The violent incident occurred on 4 February 1922. Bardoli, Gujarat: Congress leaders met on 11–12 February 1922 and resolved to suspend the planned mass civil disobedience campaign. The places had different roles in the sequence of events.

Political effects of Non-Cooperation

The movement did not immediately achieve swaraj, but it changed the character of nationalist politics.

  • Broader participation: Students, peasants, workers, traders and other groups became active in a movement extending far beyond the earlier political elite.
  • Expansion of Congress organisation: The Congress developed stronger links with local communities and gained experience in organising nationwide campaigns.
  • Swadeshi and constructive work: Khadi, hand-spinning, national education and social reform became important parts of the Gandhian programme.
  • New political awareness: Local grievances were increasingly connected with opposition to colonial rule and the demand for swaraj.
  • Limitations: Participation differed across regions and communities, maintaining non-violence was difficult, and the movement was withdrawn before its central political objective was achieved.

Two approaches within the Congress after withdrawal

The end of Non-Cooperation led to disagreement over the next method of struggle. One group supported Gandhi's emphasis on constructive work, including khadi, national education and village-level organisation.

Another group believed nationalists should enter the legislative councils and oppose colonial policies from within. Chittaranjan Das and Motilal Nehru formed the Swaraj Party in 1923 to pursue this approach while remaining connected with the wider Congress movement.

The distinction was not between supporters and opponents of Indian self-government. It concerned the political method: continuing the boycott and constructive programme, or using colonial legislative institutions as arenas of opposition.

What happened to the Khilafat issue?

The Turkish political situation also changed after the Non-Cooperation Movement ended. On 3 March 1924, the Turkish Grand National Assembly abolished the Caliphate. This removed the institution whose preservation had been the central objective of the original Khilafat agitation.

The abolition occurred after the withdrawal of Non-Cooperation in February 1922. The two events should not be confused or treated as having occurred simultaneously.

Distinguishing the main movements

MovementMain issue or methodImportant ending or transition
Rowlatt Satyagraha, 1919Non-violent protest against extraordinary repressive legislation.Gandhi suspended it in April 1919 after violence spread.
Non-Cooperation, 1920–1922Withdrawal of support from colonial institutions and foreign goods; constructive swadeshi work.Withdrawn in February 1922 following Chauri Chaura.
Khilafat agitationDefence of the Ottoman Caliph's position after the First World War.The Caliphate was abolished in Turkey in March 1924.

All 3 developments were connected to the broader nationalist movement, but each arose from a different immediate issue. Their dates, methods and outcomes must be distinguished accurately.

Prelims focus

  • Chauri Chaura incident: 4 February 1922, Gorakhpur district, United Provinces.
  • 22 policemen were killed in the Chauri Chaura incident.
  • The Congress Working Committee met at Bardoli on 11–12 February 1922.
  • The Non-Cooperation Movement was withdrawn in February 1922.
  • Chittaranjan Das and Motilal Nehru formed the Swaraj Party in 1923.
  • Turkey abolished the Caliphate on 3 March 1924.
  • Trap: The incident occurred at Chauri Chaura; the decision to suspend the proposed mass civil disobedience campaign was taken at Bardoli.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts—III, Class 8, chapter The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947, printed p. 119; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World—II, Class 10, chapter Nationalism in India, printed pp. 61–62; GandhiServe, Chronology 1922, entries for 4 February and 11–12 February, consulted 21 November 2026; Gandhi Heritage Portal, Chronology, entries for February 1922, consulted 21 November 2026; Indian National Congress, Synopsis of Plenary Sessions from 1885 to 2018, Gaya Session, 1922, and Special Delhi Session, 1923, consulted 21 November 2026; Indian National Congress, Chittaranjan Das and Swaraj Party, historical account, consulted 21 November 2026; Republic of Türkiye Ministry of Culture and Tourism, historical chronology for 1924, entry for 3 March 1924, consulted 21 November 2026.]

title: Chauri Chaura, Withdrawal in 1922 and the Political Legacy of Non-Cooperation
